pages.title: Why do neighbouring elements behave differently?

blocks.text: A metal wire conducts electricity and bends; many non-metals behave very differently. Moving across the periodic table gradually changes electronic attraction and the tendency to lose or gain electrons.
We can organise these broad categories, then use atomic and ionic size to explain some of the differences. Categories are trends, not lists without exceptions.

pages.transition: Describe the broad physical categories before explaining their trends.

pages.title: Recognise metallic and non-metallic character

blocks.text: Metals are generally lustrous, malleable, ductile and good conductors. Most are solids at room temperature. Non-metals occur as solids or gases, with bromine a liquid; they generally conduct poorly.
These are broad tendencies. Mercury is a liquid metal, graphite conducts, and some non-metals are lustrous. An observed exception does not change an element’s nuclear identity.

pages.transition: Some elements show intermediate behaviour rather than fitting one extreme.

pages.title: Understand metalloids and table location

blocks.text: Metals occupy most of the left and centre; non-metals cluster towards the upper right. Metalloids such as silicon and germanium show intermediate characteristics near the dividing region.
Metallic character generally decreases across a period and increases down a group. The trend reflects changing ease of electron loss rather than the physical location of a box causing the behaviour.

pages.transition: Size requires a careful definition because the cloud has no hard edge.

pages.title: An atom has no sharp outer edge

blocks.text: An electron cloud extends gradually, so atomic radius needs an operational definition. Covalent radius is half the internuclear distance between two identical atoms joined by a single covalent bond.
For non-bonded atoms, van der Waals radius uses their closest non-bonded contact. Metallic radius uses neighbouring nuclei in a metal. Compare like definitions; they measure different environments.

An atom’s cloud resembles a gradual distribution rather than a marble with a surface. Radius definitions choose reproducible reference distances. That is why two quoted radii may both be valid when one refers to bonding and another to non-bonded contact.

pages.transition: Use a measured bond distance to calculate a covalent radius.

pages.title: Calculate a covalent radius

blocks.text: Teacher-worked application: the Cl–Cl single-bond distance is 198 pm. Each identical atom contributes one covalent radius, so 2r=198 pm and r=99 pm.
A non-bonded chlorine contact gives a larger van der Waals radius. The difference is not a contradiction: a bonded pair can approach more closely than a non-bonded pair.

pages.transition: Now ask how comparable atomic sizes change across a period.

pages.title: Explain the decrease across a period

blocks.text: Across a main-group period, proton number increases while added electrons enter the same principal shell. Shielding does not cancel the increased nuclear attraction fully. Effective nuclear attraction therefore generally increases.
The electron cloud contracts, so atomic radius usually decreases from left to right. Do not explain this trend by saying that more electrons automatically make every atom larger.

pages.transition: A group comparison changes the principal shell as well as nuclear charge.

pages.title: Explain the increase down a group

blocks.text: Down a group, the valence electrons enter shells with larger n. Additional inner electrons provide shielding, and the outer distribution extends farther from the nucleus. Atomic size therefore generally increases.
The nucleus also gains protons, but increased shell size and shielding dominate this trend. Reasoning requires weighing competing effects rather than considering nuclear charge alone.

pages.transition: Ion formation changes electron count without changing the nucleus.

pages.title: Compare an ion with its parent atom

blocks.text: A cation is generally smaller than its parent atom: electron loss reduces repulsion and may remove the outer shell. An anion is larger because added electrons increase repulsion in the occupied valence region.
Na⁺ is smaller than Na; Cl⁻ is larger than Cl. The nucleus has not changed in either comparison. Ionic size changes because electron count and distribution change.

pages.transition: Equal electron counts let us isolate the effect of nuclear attraction.

pages.title: Rank an isoelectronic series

blocks.text: Isoelectronic species have equal electron counts. O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺ all have ten electrons, but their proton counts are 8, 9, 11, 12. More protons attract the same electron population more strongly.
Thus size decreases O²⁻>F⁻>Na⁺>Mg²⁺. First verify equal electron counts; this particular argument should not be applied to arbitrary ions with different shells.

Add Al³⁺ to the ten-electron series. It has 13 protons, so it is smaller than Mg²⁺ in the same comparison. The sequence is governed by increasing nuclear attraction for an equal electron population, not by charge labels alone.

pages.transition: Choose the right comparison before applying a size trend.

blocks.text: Use comparable radius definitions. Across a period, increasing effective attraction generally contracts atoms; down a group, extra shells enlarge them. Cations shrink and anions expand relative to their parents.
For isoelectronic species, increasing Z decreases size. These principles explain trends, while metallic and non-metallic classifications describe broad patterns with meaningful exceptions.

questions.question: Why is atomic radius not an exact hard boundary?
questions.answer: An electron cloud has no sharply defined outer surface, so radius is defined through measurable distances.

questions.question: A homonuclear single bond is 150 pm long. Find covalent radius.
Why do atoms generally shrink across a period?
questions.answer: Increasing nuclear charge is not fully shielded by same-shell additions, increasing effective attraction.

questions.question: Why do atoms grow down a group despite more protons?
questions.answer: Additional shells and shielding outweigh the increased nuclear charge for the outer electrons.

questions.question: Which is larger, Na or Na⁺?
questions.answer: Na; losing its outer electron produces a smaller cation.

questions.question: Order F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺ by increasing radius.
questions.answer: Mg²⁺<Na⁺<F⁻: all have ten electrons, but attraction strengthens with Z.

questions.question: Does good conductivity prove an element must be a metal?
questions.answer: No. Graphite is a non-metallic exception, so a single property is insufficient.
